findings.headline: Strong cash position now (£35.3m) but projected to decline to £18m within one year.
findings.detail: As at 31 March 2026, the council held £23.4m in short-term investments plus £11.9m in the current bank account. The council projects this will fall to circa £18m by 31 March 2027. While expressing confidence in meeting obligations, this trajectory reflects ongoing reserve drawdown to fund operational deficits.
findings.matters: The declining cash position, combined with the structural deficit, shows the council is already in drawdown mode. At current deficit rates, reserves would be significantly depleted by the early 2030s, tightening liquidity and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £35.3m total cash as at 31 March 2026 (£23.4m short-term investments, £11.9m current account); projected £18m by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The Council is predicting to have cash balances of circa £18m (current bank account and short-term treasury deposits) as at the 31st March 2027 and is therefore confident it can meet its financial obligations for the foreseeable future.

findings.headline: All PWLB borrowing repaid; zero long-term debt outstanding as at end of 2025/26.
findings.detail: Torridge has repaid its final Public Works Loan Board loan, leaving zero long-term borrowing commitments. The report presents this as a positive, noting only a very small proportion of revenue budget goes to capital financing costs.
findings.matters: While debt-free appears positive, for a council facing a growing £7.265m revenue deficit, the absence of an established PWLB relationship or credit line could limit borrowing options if deficits accelerate. It also signals the council has not drawn on long-term capital finance in recent years.
findings.figures: Zero long-term borrowing as at close of 2025/26; prior debts held with Public Works Loan Board
findings.quote: The balance of long-term borrowing commitments all held with the Public Works Loan Board at the close of the financial year 2026/27 was zero, the final loan having been repaid in the year.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand flagged as uncontrolled and ongoing cost risk.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is explicitly identified as a financial risk that could increase further, alongside capital programme cost overruns and pay inflation. The paper provides no quantification of current spend or trajectory, indicating it is an emerging area of concern.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is typically the fastest-growing and least controllable cost line for councils. Uncontrolled TA demand can rapidly deplete reserves and trigger unexpected budget pressures beyond forecasts.
findings.figures: No figures provided in this report
findings.quote: In particular the costs of delivering the capital programme could increase beyond the funding envelope, demand for Temporary Accommodation could increase further and pay and non-pay inflation could again return.

findings.headline: A £7.265m cumulative funding gap over 2026/27–2030/31 with only £2.001m in Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve to cover it.
findings.detail: The council's Medium Term Financial Strategy shows growing annual revenue deficits: £0.399m in 2026/27 rising to £1.932m by 2030/31. The Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve can cover only the first two years of deficits (£1.760m), leaving a £5.505m gap from 2028/29 onwards that must be closed through identified savings or new income. The paper states the council will "continue to seek operational efficiencies and new income streams in order to bring the Council's finances back into balance and therefore avoid the need to drain the Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve."
findings.matters: A structural revenue deficit that cannot be funded by existing reserves without new decisions represents material solvency risk. Without identified solutions, the council exhausts its financial buffer and faces potential financial distress.
findings.figures: £7.265m cumulative deficit; annual deficits of £0.399m (2026/27), £1.361m (2027/28), £1.679m (2028/29), £1.894m (2029/30), £1.932m (2030/31); Budgetary Stabilisation Reserve £2.001m as at 1st April 2026
findings.quote: There is therefore only enough resources in the Budgetary Stabilisation reserve to meet the cumulative deficit anticipated for the next two financial years.

findings.paper_title: DAP Annual Audit Report TDC June 2026
findings.headline: Land Charges service depends entirely on single officer with no backup, cross-training, or documented procedures
findings.detail: All Local Land Charges processing responsibilities rest with one Senior Officer, with no formal cover arrangements, no cross-trained staff, and no documented procedures. This is flagged as a 'significant resilience risk' that could disrupt service.
findings.matters: Service continuity failure could disrupt property transactions and related council revenue. Lack of documented procedures also indicates poor operational resilience.
findings.figures: 100% of Land Charges function dependent on one officer
findings.quote: A significant resilience risk exists as all processing responsibilities rest with a single officer, with no formal cover arrangements, no cross-trained staff, and no documented procedures.

findings.paper_title: DAP Annual Audit Report TDC June 2026
findings.headline: IT operational risk register has not consistently captured cyber and IT risks, creating oversight gap
findings.detail: Audit found that while ICT risks are discussed informally, the operational risk register was not capturing the full range of cyber and IT risks, 'potentially limiting oversight and effective prioritisation.' Management has since updated the register to include emerging technology and supply chain security risks.
findings.matters: Incomplete risk tracking indicates governance gaps; in a modern environment, untracked IT risks could mask or enable compromise of financial systems.
findings.figures: Operational risk register now includes emerging technology risks and supply chain dependencies (previously did not)
findings.quote: ICT risks are discussed and informally tracked, but the operational risk register has not consistently captured the full range of known and emerging cyber and IT risks potentially limiting oversight and effective prioritisation.

findings.paper_title: DAP Annual Audit Report TDC June 2026
findings.headline: Council's overall internal control environment rated Reasonable, not Substantial—indicating control gaps persist
findings.detail: Internal audit issued a 'Reasonable Assurance' opinion rather than the highest-level 'Substantial Assurance' rating. Reasonable Assurance means some issues and scope for improvement were identified that may put at risk the achievement of objectives. The report includes 11 Reasonable Assurance audits and 1 Limited Assurance audit.
findings.matters: Lenders prefer Substantial Assurance; Reasonable Assurance indicates identified control gaps that could affect the council's ability to detect or prevent financial problems and ensure accurate reporting.
findings.figures: 1 Substantial Assurance, 11 Reasonable Assurance, 1 Limited Assurance opinions issued
findings.quote: Based on work performed to date during 2025-26, our experience from previous years, the Head of Internal Audit's Opinion on the adequacy and effectiveness of the Authority's internal control framework is one of "Reasonable Assurance".

findings.paper_title: DAP Annual Audit Report TDC June 2026
findings.headline: Payroll reconciliations lack independent authorization, creating another segregation-of-duties gap
findings.detail: While payroll reconciliations are completed on a timely basis, they are not authorized by an independent officer. This means there is no independent verification that reconciliations are accurate and complete.
findings.matters: Independent authorization of financial reconciliations is a fundamental control; without it, errors or fraud in payroll could pass undetected. This is a material control weakness in a core financial process.
findings.figures: Reconciliations performed on schedule but no independent authorization required
findings.quote: Reconciliations are being undertaken in a timely manner but are currently not authorised by an independent officer.

findings.paper_title: DAP Annual Audit Report TDC June 2026
findings.headline: Payroll system has segregation of duties failure: one user holds both system admin and payroll admin access
findings.detail: Internal audit found one iTrent payroll system user has both System Administration and Payroll Administration access, violating segregation of duties principle. With only three payroll officers total, the council either needs alternative control arrangements or must formally accept this control weakness.
findings.matters: Payroll is a core financial system; lack of segregation of duties increases risk of unauthorized or fraudulent changes to employee payments. Lenders view this as evidence of weaker financial controls.
findings.figures: One user with dual access; three-person payroll team
findings.quote: There is also one user who has both System Administration and Payroll Administration access, where having access to both can lead to risks surrounding segregation of duties.

findings.headline: Inflationary pressures continuing to impact the council despite having reduced
findings.detail: The council reports that cost pressures have reduced during 2025/26, but 'not as quickly as anticipated.' Staff costs, fuel, utilities, and construction inflation remain areas of concern. These have been partially offset by Treasury Management income and grants.
findings.matters: Ongoing inflationary pressures that are reducing slower than expected constrain the council's ability to deliver cost savings and add uncertainty to budget forecasting and financial planning.
findings.figures: Specific impact figures not quantified; gains from Treasury Management and Community Regeneration Partnership grants partially offset pressures
findings.quote: These pressures have reduced during 2025/26, though not as quickly as anticipated. The areas most affected include staff costs, fuel, utilities and construction inflation.

findings.headline: Long-term financial viability identified as the council's key governance risk
findings.detail: The Statutory Finance Officer has explicitly identified long-term financial viability as the key risk area for the council's compliance with the CIPFA Financial Management Code. The council is attempting to address this through budget setting, the Medium-Term Financial Strategy, capital programme reviews, and regular financial updates to members.
findings.matters: When a council's own finance officer flags long-term viability as the primary governance risk, it signals material uncertainty about the council's ability to deliver services and meet its financial obligations in future years.
findings.figures: None provided on the scale or timeline of the viability concern
findings.quote: The Statutory Finance Officer has identified the Council's long-term financial viability as the key risk area regarding future compliance with the Code

findings.headline: A remaining funding gap that the council continues to work to close
findings.detail: The Member Budget Working Group was tasked with identifying savings and income to bring finances back towards balance. Despite producing recommendations, the statement explicitly acknowledges that 'the MBWG will continue to meet to reduce the remaining funding gap,' meaning the gap has not been closed despite ongoing work since 2022/23.
findings.matters: A council unable to close its budget gap despite three years of focused working group activity signals persistent structural imbalance that raises questions about underlying financial sustainability.
findings.figures: No specific gap figure disclosed; work has been ongoing since 2022/23
findings.quote: the MBWG will continue to meet to reduce the remaining funding gap

findings.headline: Borrowing swings from £0 forecast in 2025/26 to £8.8m planned for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's prudential borrowing profile is being reprofiled between years. The 2025/26 forecast shows £0 borrowing (against the £5.4m estimate), but 2026/27 jumps to £8.8m. This shift suggests capital schemes have been deferred or reprioritised rather than reflecting funding constraints.
findings.matters: Borrowing timing affects medium-term debt trajectory and revenue financing costs. A swing from deferred to accelerated borrowing warrants monitoring to understand capital delivery patterns and confirm financing sustainability.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Estimate £5,417k, Forecast £0k; 2026/27 Estimate £8,767k
findings.quote: Net financed by borrowing 5,417 - 8,767

findings.headline: Capital programme forecast for 2025/26 is £18.9m against estimate of £39m, a 52% shortfall
findings.detail: The council's capital programme is significantly underperforming against its approved plan. The 2025/26 forecast of £18,871k is less than half the £38,978k estimate, representing £20m of undelivered capital investment against plan. The document notes that future year estimates are 'based on the schemes approved to date' with additional schemes to be funded from own resources.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery indicates execution capability and infrastructure investment trajectory. A 50% shortfall raises questions about project delivery capability, scheme slippage, or constraints on funding or delivery.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Total Programme Estimate £38,978k, Forecast £18,871k
findings.quote: Total Programme 38,978 18,871 40,102

findings.headline: Limited authorized counterparties constrain the council's ability to achieve optimal investment rates
findings.detail: Some of Torridge's authorized investment counterparties are not accepting new deposits because they have sufficient funding, which restricts the council's ability to negotiate competitive rates on treasury placements.
findings.matters: Reduced counterparty choice means the council cannot always secure best-available rates, eroding treasury income and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: Some counterparties are not taking further deposits as they do not require further funding and this could limit our ability to invest at the most beneficial rates from time to time.

findings.headline: Treasury investment income expected to decline as both interest rates fall and investment levels shrink due to capital spending
findings.detail: The strategy anticipates that interest rates will reduce slightly during 2026/27 and that total investment balances (currently estimated at £28m) will reduce further due to continued capital expenditure. This double compression will reduce non-service revenue available to balance budgets.
findings.matters: Declining investment income reduces discretionary revenue and adds to budget pressure in the medium term, limiting financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Current investments estimated at £28m; specific forecast reductions not quantified
findings.quote: It is anticipated that the level of investments will reduce further due to continued capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Long-term PWLB borrowing rates have risen sharply, increasing the cost of any capital borrowing
findings.detail: 20-year PWLB loan rates have risen from just under 6.0% to 6.24% during 2025/26. If Torridge proceeds with the £8.85m of approved capital borrowing, it will face higher debt servicing costs than anticipated when these projects were approved.
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs reduce the financial case for capital projects and increase ongoing debt service burden, affecting sustainability of the council's capital programme.
findings.figures: 20-year PWLB rate increased to 6.24% from just under 6.0%
findings.quote: Long-term borrowing rates from the PWLB have increased during the year. The current impact of this means the interest on a 20-year loan has increase to around 6.24% from just under 6.0%.

findings.headline: £8.85m of approved capital borrowing has timing contingent on project progress and financial climate
findings.detail: Four projects have approved borrowing: Operational Service Centre (£2.8m), Town Hall Roof & Leisure Works (£1.0m), Appledore Maritime Innovation Centre (£1.1m), and Hatchmoor Industrial Estate (£3.35m). The strategy explicitly states timing is uncertain and will depend on project progress, financial climate, and internal resource availability—language suggesting either slippage or financial constraint.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether these schemes are progressing and whether the council has financial headroom to undertake £8.85m of borrowing at a time of rising rates.
findings.figures: Operational Services Centre £2.8m, Town Hall Roof & Leisure Works £1.0m, Appledore Maritime Innovation Centre £1.1m, Hatchmoor Industrial Estate £3.35m
findings.quote: The Prudential Indicators on Appendix 3 to this report have been compiled on the assumption that the borrowing will take place in the 2026/27 financial year however the timing will be dependent upon the progress made with the project, the financial climate and the availability of internal resources.

findings.headline: S151 Officer cannot provide same level of assurance for 2027/28 onwards; reserves adequacy conditioned on 'managed drawdown aligned with LGR timeline'
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states the 2026/27 budget is 'Robust' and reserves are 'adequate for 2026/27'. However, for 2027/28 onwards, the S151 states: 'I cannot provide the same level of assurance without the Member Budget Working Group identifying appropriate bridging measures.' Reserves are deemed adequate only if LGR happens on schedule and bridging measures are implemented.
findings.matters: The S151 Officer is explicitly flagging uncertainty and conditionality. For a lender, this is a signal that the council's finance officer sees 2027/28 as a point of material risk, contingent on factors outside the council's control (LGR timing) and on actions not yet taken (bridging measures).
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget assessed as 'Robust'; 2027/28 onwards assessed as contingent on bridging measures; reserves deemed adequate only for 'managed transition to LGR'
findings.quote: The budget is sufficiently robust for Members to approve with confidence for 2026/27. For 2027/28 onwards, I cannot provide the same level of assurance without the Member Budget Working Group identifying appropriate bridging measures... I assess reserves as adequate for 2026/27 and sufficient for managed transition to LGR, provided bridging measures are implemented.

findings.headline: Pay award risk: 3% assumed for 2026/27 but national negotiations ongoing; every 1% above costs £130k immediately with compounding effect
findings.detail: The budget assumes a 3% pay award for 2026/27, but the council notes 'national negotiations ongoing'. Every 1% above assumption costs £130k in year one, then grows each year due to compounding. A 4% pay award (1% above assumption) costs £130k in 2026/27, £263k cumulative by 2027/28, and £399k by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Pay awards are outside council control. If national pay bargaining produces 4% or higher, the budget deteriorates immediately. This is a near-term risk given current inflation and labour market conditions.
findings.figures: 3% pay award assumed (2026/27); 2% assumed from 2027/28 onwards; every 1% above costs £130k in 2026/27, cumulative £263k by 2027/28, £399k by 2028/29
findings.quote: Every 1% above assumption costs £130k. A 1% miscalculation costs £130k immediately, then grows each year... National Living Wage commitments drive bottom-end pay up. Local Government pay bargaining (we don't control our pay awards) can exceed budgeted amounts.

findings.headline: Planning income budgeted conservatively at £700k but is volatile and a key assumption in bridging strategy
findings.detail: Planning fee income is budgeted at £700k annually (described as 'conservative estimate') and represents a key component of the £1.6m bridging package, with assumptions of £200k above budget from planning income increases. However, the council elsewhere notes planning income is 'inherently unpredictable' and identifies it as a medium-probability, high-impact risk.
findings.matters: Planning income volatility creates execution risk in the bridging strategy. If planning activity slows (which it typically does in economic downturns), the council loses a key piece of its gap-closing plan.
findings.figures: Planning income budgeted £700k; assumed additional £200k above budget in bridging strategy; identified as 'inherently unpredictable'
findings.quote: Planning income: £700k annually (conservative estimate)... Planning income inherently unpredictable... Planning fee income (above budget) 200 [£'000]... Risk: volatile but no structural change required

findings.headline: Council Tax increases by 2.99% assumed throughout MTFS; freezing one year costs £154k/year forever, compounding to £1.6m cumulative
findings.detail: The budget assumes Council Tax rises by 2.99% (referendum limit) every year through 2030/31. If the council froze Council Tax in any single year, the loss would compound forever due to referendum rules preventing catch-up. Freezing 2027/28 would cost £645k by year 4 (£1.6m cumulative). The council is explicitly stating that Council Tax flexibility is not available as a budget management tool.
findings.matters: This removes a degree of freedom for the council. If political pressure forces a Council Tax freeze during the 2027-28 bridging period, the council loses £154k permanently, worsening the gap. The council cannot use a one-year freeze as a temporary relief measure.
findings.figures: Band D increase: 2.99% annually (£5.84 per household, 11p per week); freezing one year costs £154k/year, £645k cumulative by year 4, £1.6m over four years
findings.quote: Not increasing saves residents 11p per week but costs the Council £154k per year, forever. That £154k compounds – it's £645k lost in year 4 (£1.6M 4 year cumulative). Referendum rules mean we can never catch up on missed increases.

findings.headline: Business rates income heavily concentrated in renewable energy schemes (£1.3m = 21% of retained business rates), creating income volatility
findings.detail: Renewable energy schemes generate £1.3m annually (2026/27), representing one-fifth of all business rates Torridge retains. This income is outside the Fair Funding Review and assumed stable at inflation, but it is entirely dependent on planning decisions and the renewable energy sector. A slowdown in renewable energy planning or a shift in government policy could eliminate this revenue stream.
findings.matters: Business rates income is already the most volatile part of Torridge's funding. Concentration in one sector (renewables) amplifies that volatility. The budget bridging strategy assumes this income is stable; it is not.
findings.figures: Renewable energy schemes: £1.3m for 2026/27; represents 21% of business rates retained (£3.179m total in 2026/27)
findings.quote: Where Torridge in its capacity as the planning authority has granted consent for a renewable energy scheme, it retains 100% of the business rates payable. This is outside of the fair funding review, and equates to £1.3M for 2026/27

findings.headline: Entire financial strategy depends on Local Government Reorganisation implementing by April 2028; if delayed, more 'fundamental measures' required
findings.detail: The budget strategy explicitly abandons long-term planning and targets only a 24-month horizon to April 2028 LGR implementation. The S151 Officer states: 'If LGR is significantly delayed beyond 2028/29, temporary measures become unsustainable and more fundamental action would be required.' The council is explicitly not doing permanent service redesign because it assumes LGR makes such redesign redundant.
findings.matters: For a lender, this is a single point of failure. The council's financial plan is entirely conditional on a government decision that could change. If central government postpones LGR (which has been delayed before), Torridge's financial position deteriorates rapidly and the council's stated strategy collapses.
findings.figures: LGR expected April 2028 (24-month financial runway); if postponed beyond 2028/29, strategy requires 'more fundamental measures'
findings.quote: The LGR Context – These projections extend to 2030/31, but current LGR timelines suggest the new unitary authority (that Torridge becomes part of) will be operational by April 2028... If LGR is significantly delayed beyond 2028/29, temporary measures become unsustainable and more fundamental action would be required.

findings.headline: Structural deficit has nearly doubled to 11% (from 7% previously), requiring £1.4m in bridging measures from 2027/28
findings.detail: The structural deficit — the gap between baseline income and expenditure — has widened from 7% to 11% year-on-year. The council must identify £1.4m in savings or income generation for 2027/28 alone. The strategy relies on temporary measures (recruitment freeze, deferred projects), income growth (planning fees, car parking), and efficiency savings, but all of these are either volatile (planning), risky (car park fee increases), or time-limited.
findings.matters: An 11% structural deficit is severe. The council's proposed solutions (income growth, temporary cuts, reserve draw) are not permanent fixes. If the council must eventually address this through permanent service cuts, the scale is dramatic — £1.4m equals 37 full-time staff at average salary, or most discretionary services.
findings.quote: The structural deficit (average deficit / average funding) is now 11% (previous MTFS = 7%)... £1.4m = 37 full-time staff (at average salary) or £1.4m = Most discretionary services combined

findings.headline: Budget Stabilisation Reserve projected to run out by 2028/29, forcing reliance on uncertain Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: The council's emergency reserve, currently £2m, is projected to be exhausted by 2028/29 due to the cumulative budget gaps (£399k in 2026/27, £1.4m in 2027/28, £1.7m in 2028/29). The entire financial strategy depends on LGR implementation by April 2028, providing only a ~24 month runway. If LGR is postponed, the council will have no financial buffer.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether the council has financial resilience. Reserve depletion by 2028/29 is not hypothetical — it's the baseline scenario in the council's own MTFS. If LGR is delayed even 12 months, the council enters financial crisis.
findings.figures: Budget Stabilisation Reserve (£2m) projected to run out in 2028/29; cumulative MTFS gap £7.266m over five years
findings.quote: The reserve is currently £2m, and is used to fund the gap. It is projected to run out in 2028/29... If LGR is postponed then this approach would need to be revisited.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review permanently redistributes business rates and reduces funding by £1.7m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The government's Fair Funding Review 2.0 eliminates business rate growth that Torridge has built since 2013 and redirects funding to social care authorities. This creates a phased funding cut: £909k in 2027/28, then £350k more in 2028/29. Combined with a business rates reset, Torridge's retained business rates fall from £4.6m (2025/26) to £2.1m by 2028/29 — a £2.5m income loss within three years.
findings.matters: This is permanent structural income loss, not a temporary pressure. It fundamentally changes the council's revenue base and is the single largest driver of the growing budget gap.
findings.figures: Business rates retained fall from £4.6m (2025/26) to £2.1m by 2028/29; funding gap £400k (2026/27) rising to £1.7m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The funding redistribution is phased over 3 years. This means that a third of the lost funding crystalises each year up to 28/29... business rate growth from Torridge has been redistributed nationally

findings.paper_title: 10 - Capital Programme - Decision made at Internal Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Vehicle fleet budget increased by £2k per light van to fund transition to electric vehicles.
findings.detail: The council voted to increase the vehicle programme budget by £2k per light van specifically to support a planned transition to electric vehicles. This represents a deliberate policy shift with capital cost implications.
findings.matters: Fleet electrification decisions affect capital spending, operational costs (charging infrastructure, maintenance), and the council's longer-term financial sustainability and sustainability commitments.
findings.figures: £2k per light van
findings.quote: Increase the vehicle programme by an additional £2k per light van to support the transition to electric vehicles.

findings.paper_title: 10 - Capital Programme - Decision made at Internal Overview and Scrutiny Committee
findings.headline: Four new capital projects approved: server infrastructure, two energy-saving schemes, and building control system.
findings.detail: The council approved new capital commitments: a server room generator (£33k), energy saving works at Appledore Fish dock (£140k), TDC energy saving works (£200k), and a Building Control back-office system (£77k). These add to the capital programme 2026/27–2030/31.
findings.matters: New capital projects increase the council's debt service obligations and affect borrowing requirements. Energy spending indicates efficiency investments; the building control system suggests operational IT transformation.
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is updated to include four new projects: Generator for Server Room - £33k, Appledore Fish dock Energy Saving Works - £140k, TDC Energy Saving Works - £200k, Building Control – New Back-office System – Dataspace - £77k

findings.headline: Capital programme deliverability at risk from inflation-driven funding gaps requiring member decisions
findings.detail: The strategy states that the capital programme is regularly updated for inflation, which can create funding shortfalls. When gaps occur, members must decide how to close them, potentially through project deferral, redesign, or cancellation. No current gap is reported, but the process acknowledges programme deliverability is contingent on managing this risk.
findings.matters: Indicates capital programme of £65.5m may not be fully deliverable if inflation persists; a lender needs to understand which projects are discretionary versus statutory.
findings.figures: £65.5m total capital expenditure plan
findings.quote: The capital programme and subsequent funding, is regularly updated to reflect inflation. This can result in a funding shortfall / funding gap, if/when this occurs then members are consulted to look for ways to close any shortfall/gap.

findings.headline: £5.5m new borrowing authorised with £330,000 annual interest costs
findings.detail: The council has authorised external borrowing totalling £5.5m to fund four major initiatives: Operational Service Centre (£2.8m), Town Hall Roof & Leisure works (£1.0m), Appledore Clean Maritime Innovation Centre (£1.1m), and a Community Land Trusts revolving loan fund (£600k). Annual interest payable calculated at £330,000.
findings.matters: The council is taking on material new borrowing with an ongoing annual interest cost of £330,000; business cases must demonstrate that projects generate sufficient returns to cover interest and Minimum Revenue Provision costs.
findings.figures: £5.5m total borrowing; £330,000 annual interest; individual projects £2.8m, £1.0m, £1.1m, £600,000
findings.quote: Based on the projected borrowing discussed above of £5.5m for the new Operational Service Centre, Town Hall roof works, Appledore Clean Maritime Innovation Centre & CLT revolving loan fund, and a maturity structure which is spread to mitigate against interest rate risk, it is calculated that interest payable would be £330k per year.

findings.headline: Council committed to net zero carbon by 2030 but cannot quantify implementation costs
findings.detail: The council has declared a Climate Emergency and committed to net zero carbon emissions from operations by 2030. The strategy explicitly acknowledges this will require additional capital and revenue costs, but states these cannot yet be quantified. This represents a material unquantified future liability.
findings.matters: Material unquantified future costs could significantly impact capital programme delivery and/or require future revenue budget pressures; a lender needs to understand the scale of this unquantified commitment.
findings.figures: Net zero target: 2030
findings.quote: This 'Climate Emergency' will have an impact on our capital programme, and capital strategy going forward, resulting in extra costs and commitments. These additional costs and commitments are not quantifiable at this time.

findings.headline: Capital projects are being reviewed against Local Government Reform deadline of April 2028, creating strategic uncertainty
findings.detail: Officers are explicitly reviewing PIDs to ensure they provide lasting benefit to Torridge beyond April 2028, indicating that council structure is expected to change or be uncertain at that point. This affects whether capital schemes need to be future-proofed or may be orphaned.
findings.matters: Structural reform creates uncertainty about which assets the council will own and operate; affects long-term capital strategy and borrowing assumptions
findings.figures: April 2028 reform deadline
findings.quote: Project Initiation Documents should be reviewed with Local Government Reform in mind, ensuring that any proposed additions to the capital programme provide lasting benefit to Torridge District beyond April 2028.

findings.headline: Capital programme includes £48k additional investment to transition light van fleet to electric vehicles
findings.detail: The council is adding £2k per light van beyond base replacement cost to support transition to electric. This is being built into the capital programme as a specific climate/net-zero commitment, not a budgeted saving.
findings.matters: Shows capital cost of decarbonisation is being factored in; also indicates ongoing capex pressure as vehicle replacement cycles require higher upfront investment
findings.figures: £2k per light van; £48k total over the period
findings.quote: This includes a proposal to include an additional £2k per light van to support the transition to electric vehicles, adding a further £48k to the programme over the above-mentioned period.

findings.headline: Council rejected parking enforcement system project (£39k) because it scored 55 against 65-point minimum threshold
findings.detail: Of five proposed new projects, the council has recommended excluding Unity 5 – Parking enforcement system because its project score (55) fell below the recommended minimum of 65. This shows capital discipline but also that the council had to deprioritise something it wanted to fund.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council is applying rigorous capital prioritization standards; also indicates the council is already at the limit of what it can fund within the priority threshold
findings.figures: £39k; project score 55 vs 65 minimum
findings.quote: Note: A minimum score of 65 is recommended for inclusion into the capital programme, therefore with Unity 5 – Parking enforcement system having only achieved a project score of 55, we would recommend it is excluded from the capital programme for 2026.27.

findings.headline: Leisure centre running costs of £60k per site per year identified as significant ongoing future pressure
findings.detail: The report flags leisure centre costs (for three centres) as a material pressure on the capital programme alongside inflation, net zero transition, and linear defence partnership costs. This appears to be an unfunded or only partially funded commitment being tracked as a constraint on capital deployment.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director needs to know whether the council can sustain these three leisure centres or is facing difficult decisions on closure, subsidy levels, or capital replacement.
findings.figures: £60k per site per year (implying c. £180k+ annually for three centres)
findings.quote: Whilst also considering other significant future pressures, including - Leisure (3 centres, estimates of £60K per site per year)

findings.headline: Council has £8.767m approved borrowing and is explicitly directing capital surplus to reduce future borrowing requirement
findings.detail: The report identifies a £1.339m surplus on the general capital programme and recommends applying it to reduce approved borrowing. The council states this will lower future interest costs and reduce ongoing revenue pressure from capital financing charges. This is an active financial strategy decision, not a passive funding position.
findings.matters: Capital financing charges are an ongoing revenue cost; strategic reduction of borrowing directly improves future-year affordability and budget flexibility
findings.figures: £8.767m approved borrowing; £1.339m general programme surplus
findings.quote: With £8.767m (Appendix 2) of approved borrowing within the Capital Programme, it would be prudent to consider applying a proportion of the identified surplus capital to reduce the Council's future borrowing requirement. Redirecting surplus resources in this way will lower future interest costs and, in turn, reduce the ongoing pressure placed on the revenue budget through capital financing charges.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to decline from £831k to £725k as interest rates fall
findings.detail: Despite holding more cash, investment returns are falling because interest rates have declined. The average return forecast is 4.62% for 2025/26 compared to 5.35% last year. The Bank of England has cut rates five times since August 2024 and is currently holding them at 4%.
findings.matters: A material reduction in investment income of £106k year-on-year creates a funding gap that must be compensated elsewhere in the budget and reduces the council's financial flexibility
findings.figures: £725k (2025/26 forecast), £831k (2024/25), 4.62% forecast rate vs 5.35% prior year
findings.quote: The average rate of return earned by the Council on its short term investments is forecast to be 4.62% which compares with 5.35% in 2024/25. The forecasted return from short term investments for 2025/26 is £725k, which compares with a return of £831k in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Short-term investment holdings more than doubled to £33m from £15m in one year
findings.detail: The council's liquid investments have increased significantly to £33m compared to £15m the same time last year, spread to take best advantage of interest rates. The paper does not explain the reason for this substantial increase.
findings.matters: A doubling of cash holdings raises questions about whether this reflects improved cash generation or deferred expenditure; understanding the driver is material to assessing the council's financial position
findings.figures: £33m (current), £15m (prior year)
findings.quote: Currently the Council has short term investments of £33m lodged with financial institutions, the comparable figure for the same time last year being £15m.

findings.headline: £3.35m additional borrowing for Hatchmoor Project approved but not yet drawn
findings.detail: Full Council approved this additional borrowing for capital works in September 2025. The borrowing has not yet been actioned because the project is still in its initial phase, meaning the council has a committed but undrawn borrowing facility that will increase debt when drawn.
findings.matters: This represents a future liability and capital commitment; project delivery pace and any cost overruns are material risks to the council's financial position
findings.quote: On the 22nd September 2025, members of Full Council approved £3.35m of additional future borrowing for the additional capital works on the Hatchmoor Project. The borrowing has not yet been actioned as the project is still in its initial phase.

findings.headline: IFRS16 accounting change adds £1.046m in lease liabilities to the council's balance sheet.
findings.detail: New accounting standard (effective 1 April 2024) requires all material operating leases to be recorded as right-of-use assets and corresponding liabilities. Torridge has calculated £1,046K in lease liabilities, primarily from private sector housing leases, which are now classified as long-term liabilities equivalent to borrowing.
findings.matters: Increases reported total debt and affects financial ratios and covenant compliance that lenders monitor when assessing financial health.
findings.figures: £1,046K in lease liabilities calculated
findings.quote: A borrowing figure for these leases of £1,046K has been calculated and included in the prudential indicators.

findings.headline: Long-term PWLB borrowing rates increased by 0.5% on 20-year loans, raising cost of planned borrowing.
findings.detail: PWLB rates on 20-year loans rose from just under 5.5% to around 6.0% during 2024/25. This rate increase applies directly to the council's planned £5.5m borrowing program, materially increasing the annual revenue cost of debt service and reducing project affordability.
findings.matters: Higher borrowing costs reduce the net benefit of capital projects and increase ongoing revenue pressure; affects the financial case for the borrowing program.
findings.figures: 20-year PWLB rate increased from ~5.5% to ~6.0%
findings.quote: Long term borrowing rates from the PWLB have increased during the year. The current impact of this means the interest on a 20 year loan has increase to around 6.0% from just under 5.5%

findings.headline: Council planning £5.5m in new PWLB borrowing for four major capital projects in 2025/26.
findings.detail: Approved borrowing comprises Operational Services Centre (£2.8m), Town Hall Roof & Leisure Works (£1.0m), Appledore Clean Maritime Innovation Centre (£1.1m), and Community Land Trust revolving fund (£0.6m). Actual draw-down timing will depend on project progress, financial climate, and availability of internal resources. Current PWLB debt is minimal at £0.191m with final redemption in March 2027.
findings.matters: This represents a material increase in the council's debt burden and will significantly increase annual revenue debt servicing costs, affecting medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £2.8m, £1.0m, £1.1m, £0.6m (total £5.5m approved); current PWLB debt £0.191m
findings.quote: The approved Prudential Indicators envisage that substantial further long-term borrowing may be undertaken in the year 2025/26 relating to the new Operational Service Centre, Town Hall Roof, and Appledore Clean Maritime Innovation Centre.

findings.headline: Council holds £14.6m net investment surplus with minimal borrowing, generating net interest income instead of cost
findings.detail: Investments of £15,268k substantially exceed borrowing of £713k (net borrowing -£14,555k). This is well below both the CFR and the authorized limit of £10.5m. All borrowing is fixed rate. The interest received on investments exceeds financing costs by approximately £1.2m.
findings.matters: The large cash surplus reflects the deferred capital spending. Lenders need to understand whether this represents strong financial management or weak capital deployment, and whether interest income sustainability depends on holding large undeployed cash reserves.
findings.figures: Investments £15,268k; borrowing £713k; net financing income £1,165k; net borrowing position -£14,555k vs CFR of £1,822k.
findings.quote: The above table clearly shows that the Council's net borrowing is significantly less that the Capital Financing Requirement as shown in 3, thus confirming that borrowing was for capital purposes only.

findings.headline: Major capital project significantly delayed; £26.9m planned spend fell to £6.4m, deferring £2.8m borrowing to future years
findings.detail: The Operational Services Centre project came in at 76% below budget. Capital expenditure was £6,411k against the estimate of £26,867k. The paper explicitly states that £2.8m of planned external borrowing for this project has been delayed into future years, altering the council's debt trajectory.
findings.matters: A project delay of this scale signals execution risk and changes the council's medium-term borrowing and debt service position. It raises questions about planning, budget, or delivery capability.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure estimated at £26,867k; actual £6,411k. £2.8m of Operational Services Centre borrowing delayed.
findings.quote: The variance between actual and estimated capital expenditure is due to the delay in spend on the new Operational Services Centre. * £2.8m of external borrowing relating to the new Operational Service Centre was delayed until future years.

news_drafts.headline: Strong cash position now (£35.3m) but projected to decline to £18m within one year.
news_drafts.lead: The declining cash position, combined with the structural deficit, shows the council is already in drawdown mode. At current deficit rates, reserves would be significantly depleted by the early 2030s, tightening liquidity and financial flexibility.

news_drafts.headline: All PWLB borrowing repaid; zero long-term debt outstanding as at end of 2025/26.
news_drafts.lead: While debt-free appears positive, for a council facing a growing £7.265m revenue deficit, the absence of an established PWLB relationship or credit line could limit borrowing options if deficits accelerate. It also signals the council has not drawn on…

news_drafts.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand flagged as uncontrolled and ongoing cost risk.
news_drafts.lead: Temporary Accommodation is typically the fastest-growing and least controllable cost line for councils. Uncontrolled TA demand can rapidly deplete reserves and trigger unexpected budget pressures beyond forecasts.
